Part D Runtime · Chapter 10

Runtime and human-in-the-loop

How an agent carries information that is not part of the conversation (runtime), how state differs from context, and how to pause for a human with approve, edit, reject and respond, including interrupts that fire only on certain data.

Class 1522 August45 min readCode: Weekend 09
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Two interview favourites live here. First, state vs runtime context: many learners mix them up, and even the instructor first answered one question the wrong way round before correcting it. Second, human-in-the-loop: an unguarded cancel_booking agent cancels anyone's booking with no questions asked, which is exactly why certain actions need a human.

Core ideas

1. State, recapped

Every agent manages its execution through AgentState, a typed dictionary holding the conversation history plus any custom fields tools or middleware need. It ships with messages and can be extended by inheriting from AgentState. It powers every node-style hook (before_model, after_model), which receive and can return updates to it.

2. The problem runtime solves

CineBot must know things that are not part of the conversation: which customer is talking, whether they are a VIP, which cinema location this is. ChatGPT and Claude know your tier and name without you typing them into the chat.

AnalogyThe hospital wristband

A patient gets a wristband. The ER doctor, the pharmacist, every nurse can read it and know who the patient is, which room they are in and their history, without the patient explaining each time. That information is not part of any single conversation. It travels with the patient. Runtime is that wristband: information outside the conversation that goes into every tool call and every middleware hook.

3. The five components of runtime

create_agent runs on LangGraph's runtime. LangChain exposes what LangGraph already maintains. Every framework has an equivalent under another name (Google's ADK and various agent CLIs), so the idea transfers.

4. Defining context: context_schema

from dataclasses import dataclass
from langchain.agents import create_agent

@dataclass
class CineBotContext:
    user_name: str

agent_with_context = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[],
    context_schema=CineBotContext,          # the SHAPE of context this agent expects
)

result = agent_with_context.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What's my name?"}]},
    context=CineBotContext(user_name="Priya"),   # injected at invocation time
)

context_schema is a skeleton: the shape of per-run information, defined once. Passing context= injects it without it appearing in the conversation. Passing it does not automatically make the agent use it in replies. You must make that link deliberately (see dynamic prompts below).

5. Runtime inside tools: ToolRuntime

from langchain.tools import tool, ToolRuntime
from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore

@dataclass
class CustomerContext:
    user_id: str

loyalty_store = InMemoryStore()

@tool
def fetch_customer_preferences(runtime: ToolRuntime[CustomerContext]) -> str:
    "Fetch the customer's saved preferences from long-term memory"
    user_id = runtime.context.user_id
    preferences = "No preferences"
    if runtime.store:
        if memory := runtime.store.get(("users"), user_id):
            preferences = memory.value["preferences"]
    return preferences

pref_agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[fetch_customer_preferences],
    context_schema=CustomerContext,
    store=loyalty_store,
)

The user id travels in runtime.context.user_id and the tool reads long-term preferences from the store, with the user never stating any of it. This is how Claude "remembers" your name across sessions: it lives in a store, reached through runtime, separate from message history.

Why ToolRuntime and not the raw runtime? LangChain's choice: a tool never gets a shared store object lying around. It gets a tool_runtime parameter, deliberately passed, holding the five components plus tool extras (state, config, tool call id). A tool sees only what it is explicitly handed.

6. Who gets what

Where What it receives
Tool ToolRuntime bundling runtime and state, plus config and tool call id
Node-style hook (before_model, after_model) state and runtime as two separate parameters
Wrap-style hook (wrap_model_call) One request (ModelRequest) that contains state and runtime

None of this is opt-in. A hook defined with zero parameters failed live with "takes 0 positional arguments but 2 were given". Parameter names do not matter (a, b works like state, runtime), only position and count.

Key ideaState vs context: mutability and persistence

State is mutable and persists across multiple invocations within the same conversation. Use it for anything that changes over time, such as a running call count.

Context is immutable per run. Use it for static values such as a user id or database credentials.

Only state changes carry forward across multiple tool calls within one invocation. Context stays fixed throughout. The instructor first stated this the wrong way round in class, caught it at the break and corrected it. Learn it carefully.

7. Dynamic prompts from runtime

from langchain.agents.middleware import dynamic_prompt

@dynamic_prompt
def personalize_the_prompt(request: ModelRequest):
    user_name = request.runtime.context.user_name
    return f"You are CineBot. Always address the user as {user_name}."

This is the mechanism behind a chat assistant that greets a returning user by name without it being typed in this conversation. The prompt is rebuilt on every call from runtime values.

8. An authorisation gate

from langchain.agents.middleware import before_model

@before_model
def auth_gate(state: AgentState, runtime: Runtime) -> dict | None:
    "Block unauthenticated users"
    server = runtime.server_info
    if server is not None:
        raise ValueError("Unauthenticated user")
    print(f"[AUTH] Passed for user {runtime.context.user_name} "
          f"and thread {runtime.execution_info.thread_id}")

It combines execution_info.thread_id (which run is this) and server_info (is this a LangGraph server context) to gate a model call before it is allowed.

Human-in-the-loop in depth

Agents run in the agentic loop. HITL is the moment a human is deliberately brought into that loop.

9. The motivating problem

@tool
def cancel_booking(booking_id: str) -> str:
    """Cancel an existing booking. Irreversible."""
    return f"Booking {booking_id} cancelled."

unguarded_agent = create_agent(model="openai:gpt-5.5", tools=[cancel_booking])
unguarded_agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Cancel my booking BK1042")]})

It cancels immediately. Anyone who can talk to this agent can cancel anyone's booking. Certain actions are too consequential to let an agent complete without confirmation.

10. Guarding the tool

from langchain.agents.middleware import HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langgraph.types import Command

guarded_agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[cancel_booking, send_booking_confirmation],
    middleware=[
        HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(
            interrupt_on={
                "cancel_booking": True,               # all four decisions allowed
                "send_booking_confirmation": False,   # safe: never pauses
            },
            description_prefix="CineBot action pending your approval",
        ),
    ],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),    # REQUIRED: pause now, resume later
)

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "hitl-demo-111"}}
result = guarded_agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [("user", "Cancel booking BK1042")]},
    config=config,
    version="v2",     # the current, recommended pattern for reading interrupts
)

HITL pauses and resumes, so it needs the checkpointer and thread_id. Without them there is nothing to resume into. Checking result.interrupts shows an action_request with the tool name, arguments, description and allowed decisions (approve, edit, reject or respond). The False tool never interrupts.

11. Command: answering an interrupt

resumed = guarded_agent.invoke(
    Command(resume={"decisions": [{"type": "approve"}]}),
    config=config,         # the SAME thread id resumes the paused run
    version="v2",
)

12. The four decisions

Decision What happens Example
approve Runs the original call unchanged Confirm the cancellation
edit Changes the arguments, then runs Cancel a different booking id
reject Skips execution, with a reason "Requires manager sign-off"
respond Replies without calling the tool Answer a clarifying question the agent asked 
# edit
Command(resume={"decisions": [{
    "type": "edit",
    "edited_action": {"name": "cancel_booking", "args": {"booking_id": "BK1042"}},
}]})

# reject
Command(resume={"decisions": [{
    "type": "reject",
    "message": "Cancellations require manager sign-off first. Ask the customer to call support.",
}]})

respond is the one new decision. It is for tools that are really asking the user something:

@tool
def ask_customer(question: str) -> str:
    """Ask the customer a clarifying question and wait for their reply."""
    return "placeholder: never reached, respond intercepts this"

ask_agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[ask_customer],
    middleware=[HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(
        interrupt_on={"ask_customer": {"allowed_decisions": ["respond"]}})],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

Command(resume={"decisions": [{"type": "respond",
        "message": "It's booking BK1042, for the movie Interstellar"}]})

The tool result is skipped and the human's message goes back to the agent as if the tool produced it. It is a genuine two-way conversation, like Claude pausing to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing. The human is not approving anything; they are supplying missing information.

13. Conditional interrupts

An e-commerce company wants a human only when an order crosses a threshold, not for every cancellation.

from langchain.agents.middleware import ToolCallRequest

def is_large_refund(request: ToolCallRequest) -> bool:
    amount = request.tool_call["args"].get("amount", 0)
    return amount > 100

conditional_agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    tools=[cancel_booking_priced],
    middleware=[HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={
        "cancel_booking_priced": {
            "allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"],
            "when": is_large_refund,
        },
    })],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

ToolCallRequest (the object underneath wrap_tool_call) carries tool_call, tool, state and runtime, enough to inspect the actual arguments. A $25 refund sailed through with no interrupt. A $500 refund on the same tool and middleware paused for approval. The interrupt depends on the data in that specific call.

The session's diagram shows the production version: cancelling booking BK1011 worth $101 pauses for an executive (not the customer) to approve, mirroring a real refund workflow.

14. The interactive loop

def run_interactive_hitl(agent, config):
    result = agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Cancel booking BK1042")]},
                          config=config, version="v2")
    if not result.interrupts:
        return
    choice = input("1) approve  2) edit  3) reject: ").strip()
    if choice == "1":
        decision = {"type": "approve"}
    elif choice == "2":
        new_id = input("Booking ID to cancel instead: ").strip()
        decision = {"type": "edit",
                    "edited_action": {"name": "cancel_booking", "args": {"booking_id": new_id}}}
    else:
        decision = {"type": "reject", "message": input("Reason: ").strip()}
    resumed = agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [decision]}), config=config, version="v2")
    print(resumed.value["messages"][-1].content)

A real UI replaces input() with buttons, as in Claude's interface, but the loop is identical in any framework: invoke, check for interrupts, collect a decision, resume with a Command. The same four ideas appear under different names elsewhere.

Questions from class worth knowing

My agent has a response_format and tools. Why does even "hi" come back structured?

Expected. Once structured output is configured the agent always tries to shape its final answer that way. That is separate from a tool's return_direct, which controls whether the tool's raw result skips the model.

Does the order of ToolErrorMiddleware and ToolRetryMiddleware matter?

Yes. Retry has to be resolved before an error is finally reported, so declare retry ahead of error handling. The other way can cause confusing looping rather than "retry a few times, then report".

Is MCP the same as defining tools in LangChain?

In a simple sense, yes: MCP is a collection of tools in a standard protocol. The "agent calls a tool" mechanic does not change. MCP changes how tools are packaged, discovered and shared across applications.

RAG or fine-tuning to keep a model current with changing company policy?

RAG. Fine-tuning is expensive and slow and will not reliably track fast-changing policy. RAG handles frequently updated reference material far better.

Is RAG always needed for agent memory?

No. If you simply persist and look up structured data, a plain database read through LangChain works as well. RAG fits when you retrieve documents by meaning.

How do you cut tokens in a long-running conversation?

Use long-term memory (the store via runtime). Retrieve only memories relevant to the current message instead of loading the whole history. Whether to load everything, load selectively or summarise is a design decision LangChain does not make for you.

Can decorated middleware functions have any name?

Decorator-based: yes, any name, because the decorator registers the hook. Class-based: no, the method name must match the hook it overrides (for example before_model).

What does an interviewer for agentic roles care about?

Software engineering fundamentals and problem solving over memorised syntax. You should explain why code does what it does, including basics such as what Pydantic is for. Someone strong in general development can integrate AI anywhere; the reverse leaves a real gap.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Confusing state and context Values reset, or cannot be changed State is mutable and persists; context is immutable per run
Expecting passed context to appear in replies The agent ignores it Use it deliberately, for example in a dynamic prompt
HITL without a checkpointer or thread id Cannot resume Add InMemorySaver and reuse the thread id
Resuming with a different thread id Starts a new run Reuse the same id
Interrupting every call Humans overloaded Add a when condition on the arguments
Using respond to approve an action Tool skipped respond supplies information; use approve to run
Hook with no parameters "takes 0 positional arguments but 2 were given" Accept state and runtime
Putting secrets in state Saved in checkpoints Keep static secrets in context or the app

Hands-on lab

  1. Build CineBotContext, pass context= at invoke time and confirm it is usable without being in the conversation.
  2. Build fetch_customer_preferences with ToolRuntime and InMemoryStore. Confirm persistence across separate invokes.
  3. Define a zero-parameter hook and watch it fail.
  4. Build the dynamic_prompt example and confirm the prompt changes with context.
  5. Compare unguarded_agent and guarded_agent.
  6. Run all four decisions: approve, edit, reject, respond.
  7. Build is_large_refund and compare a small and a large amount.
  8. Test mutability: change a value in context mid-run (it should not stick) and in state (it should persist across tool calls).

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

State holds the conversation and mutable custom fields and persists across invocations in a thread. Runtime holds what travels with the agent but is not conversation: immutable context, a long-term store, a stream writer, execution info and server info. For risky tool calls I add human-in-the-loop middleware with a checkpointer: the agent pauses, and I resume the same thread with a Command carrying approve, edit, reject or respond. I can make the interrupt conditional on the tool's arguments.

Basics

What is runtime, and what are its five components?

Information that is not part of the conversation but travels with the agent into every tool and hook: context, store, stream_writer, execution_info and server_info. Hospital wristband analogy.

What are the four HITL decisions?

approve (run unchanged), edit (change arguments then run), reject (skip, with a reason) and respond (answer without calling the tool, for clarifying questions).

Why does HITL need a checkpointer?

The agent pauses mid-run and resumes later. The checkpointer saves state and the thread_id finds it again. Without them there is nothing to resume.

What does Command(resume=...) do?

It is the answer to an interrupt. Invoke the same thread with it and the agent continues according to the decision.

Intermediate

State vs context?

State is mutable and persists across invocations in a conversation (for example a running count). Context is immutable per run (a user id or credentials). Only state changes carry across tool calls in one invocation.

How does a tool access runtime?

By declaring a runtime: ToolRuntime parameter. It bundles the runtime components with state, config and tool call id. It is hidden from the model's schema. A tool never receives the raw shared store directly.

What do hooks receive?

Node-style hooks (before_model, after_model) get state and runtime as two parameters. Wrap-style hooks (wrap_model_call) get one request object containing both. Names do not matter, position and count do.

How do you personalise the system prompt per user?

A @dynamic_prompt function that reads request.runtime.context and returns a prompt, rebuilt on every call.

How do you interrupt only for large refunds?

Add a when callable to interrupt_on that inspects request.tool_call["args"] and returns True when the amount exceeds the threshold. Small refunds run; large ones pause.

Tricky

What is respond for, and how is it different from approve?

respond is for tools that are really asking the user something. It skips the tool and feeds the human's message back as if the tool returned it. approve runs the original tool call.

Can an agent change a context value mid-run?

No. Context is immutable per run. If a value must change, it belongs in state.

Why not give tools the raw runtime object?

LangChain deliberately controls what each component receives. Tools get ToolRuntime, so they see only what they are explicitly handed.

Why might an agent ask for approval twice after you edit an amount?

That is the model's own judgment: after a partial transfer it decided a remaining balance needed handling. It is not scripted behaviour of the middleware.

When do you stop using HITL's interrupt_on shortcuts and write custom middleware?

For needs the middleware does not offer, such as two levels of sign-off. Then write custom middleware (Chapter 9).

Part E MCP · Chapter 11

Why MCP exists

The story of a brain with no hands, why function calling stopped scaling, and how the Model Context Protocol fixes it with a host, client and server architecture and three primitives: tools, resources and prompts.

Class 1623 August40 min readCode: Weekend 09
Jump to a section

Why it matters

MCP only makes sense in light of the problem before it. Interviews ask "why MCP when I have function calling?" and "what are the three primitives?" Candidates who only know the definition get stuck on the follow-ups. This chapter gives you the story, the architecture and the vocabulary.

Key ideaThe one line to anchor everything

MCP is not about giving the LLM more intelligence. It is about giving it the ability to see more.

That is why "context" is in the name: Model, Context, Protocol. The new piece is the protocol, which makes sharing context standard instead of ad hoc.

Core ideas

1. From black box to hands

  • The brain with no hands. The first ChatGPT was an LLM, a next-token predictor. It could write a leave email but could not send it. ChatGPT reached about a million users in a week and about 100 million in a few months; before that, machines mostly understood fixed inputs like buttons.
  • Step 1: function calling (mid 2023). OpenAI let you bind tools to the model. You describe an action ("send email") and the model says which function to call with which arguments. The model never executes anything. No more copy-pasting between ChatGPT and your inbox.
  • Step 2: the scaling problem. A company runs three assistants (general chatbot, coding, analytics) each touching about 20 tools across several apps. That is dozens of tools, each with its own auth, data format, error handling and breakage risk when the API changes. Multiply across every company doing this alone. As the instructor put it, we found a shorter way, but now need a complete thing to keep the shortcut running.
  • Step 3: Anthropic's answer. Not another wrapper but a protocol, a shared language like HTTP for the web. An app exposes its tools, resources and prompts once, and any AI host can speak to it the same way.

2. What MCP is

An open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems: data sources, local files, databases, tools, search engines, calculators, workflows and specialised prompts.

The instructor avoided the common "USB-C port" analogy as an oversimplification. His framing: an MCP server is a collection of tools (used about 99% of the time), wrapped around APIs that already existed, plus two other pieces: resources and prompts. All three are MCP primitives.

3. Before vs after MCP

Before MCP (raw tools or functions) After MCP
Defining an integration Easy for one API: any LLM can write a quick Gmail wrapper Easy to connect: point your host at the server
Maintenance Every team writes and maintains its own wrapper, violating DRY at scale Sits with whoever runs the server, usually the provider
Change management If Gmail changes its API, every integrator updates their code The server absorbs the change; clients touch nothing
Security Every tool needs its own auth handling, owned by you Still needs auth, but centralised at the server
Key ideaThe real trade-off

At 500 teams each wrapping the same "send email" API, you have not saved effort, you have relocated it. MCP's value is not a new capability. It is who is responsible for keeping the integration working.

4. Architecture: host, client, server

The host is the application a person uses (Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, any LangChain, LangGraph or AutoGen app). It does not talk to a server directly. It starts an MCP client internally, and that client does the talking.

AnalogyTwo analogies, hold both

Phone and network: the phone is the host, the network is the server, and the SIM card is the client in between. The phone cannot reach the network without one.

Universal remote: a remote in a house full of smart gadgets, with an adapter behind each one translating button presses. The person holding the remote is the host. They never rewire a gadget; they press a button and something else handles the rest.

The host never talks to a server directly. If every host had to know the wiring of every tool, adding one capability would be an engineering project each time. A host only needs to know how to ask.

One client per server. The host creates a dedicated client for each server, and each client keeps a private 1:1 connection to exactly one server. A host connected to five servers runs five clients, never one shared line.

Local servers typically serve one client; remote servers typically serve many.

Why dedicated connections Meaning
Decoupling Changing one server never requires touching how the host talks to another
Safety A crash stays inside one connection. The notebook proves it: start server.py, connect Inspector, press Ctrl+C in the server's terminal. Inspector does not crash; it shows that one connection closed. With five servers, killing one leaves four untouched
Scalability A heavily loaded server's growth is local to its client-server pair
Parallelism Three live connections can be used at once instead of taking turns on one shared line

5. The transport layer

Client and server speak JSON-RPC 2.0, not plain REST. Asked "is MCP just a REST client?", the answer was: at a high level you can think of it that way, but it is a distinct protocol with its own transport rules.

Transport Used for
STDIO (standard input and output) Servers running locally on your own machine
Streamable HTTP Remote or hosted servers. It replaced the older HTTP plus SSE transport, deprecated in the spec released in March 2025 (the practical cutoff varies by server)
Common trapTool lists cost tokens

Connecting even two MCP servers to Claude added a large chunk of tokens to a single "hi", because the entire tool list from every connected server is sent up front. Claude's context inspector showed tens of thousands of tokens for custom tools with just two servers. Mitigate with good tool descriptions and with middleware or interceptors that trim the list to what is relevant (the dynamic loading ideas from Chapters 6 and 8).

6. The three primitives

Primitive What it is Analogy Why it exists
Tools Executable actions with a real effect A button that does something The only primitive that lets the AI do something rather than describe it. add runs logic and produces a new result
Resources Read-only reference data, no side effects The digital display on a thermostat: you glance, you do not ask Without it every client hard-codes its own copy and the copies drift apart. One resource read fresh means one copy of the truth
Prompts Reusable templates that shape how a request is phrased A form with blank fields Consistency that survives who is asking. The structure lives once on the server

Prompts example. An AI logging a support escalation with no guidance might write "customer unhappy, refund maybe". A server template requiring four fields (issue, what was tried, customer sentiment, recommended next step) gives the same structure every time. The model did not change; the form did.

NoteCode for resources and prompts comes later

This class covered the shape and reasoning of all three, with running code only for tools. Full resources and prompts code arrives in Chapter 12.

Live demo: a local server end to end

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh                 # macOS and Linux
uv init mcp-warmup && cd mcp-warmup
uv add fastmcp

from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Warm-Up Server")

@mcp.tool
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """Greet someone by name."""
    return f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to MCP."

@mcp.tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers together."""
    return a + b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

No special boilerplate beyond @mcp.tool. FastMCP reads each function's docstring as the tool description, which is what appeared in Inspector's tool list.

Run it with the Inspector:

uv run fastmcp dev server.py        # opens MCP Inspector at http://127.0.0.1:6274

Inspector is a browser tool that connects to any MCP server and lets you call its tools directly, acting as host plus client. Calling greet and add is two real programs completing a task over the actual protocol.

Wire it into real hosts:

  • VS Code: register the server as STDIO with the launch command uv run python server.py and the working directory set to the folder with server.py. VS Code records it in mcp.json and a new chat can call greet and add.
  • Claude Desktop: Manage Connectors, then Add custom connector, pointing at a remote server URL (or the local pattern).

Same server, any host, no changes. That was the point.

Pro tipSharing a local server

A local server can be shared with a small team by port-forwarding or tunnelling it, though that is not the most secure option. Team-wide hosting and publishing to PyPI come in later classes.

Questions from class worth knowing

How is MCP different from calling a REST API directly?

The end result can be the same, but with a raw API you maintain the wrapper, auth and error handling in every project. With MCP, the server owner maintains it once and every AI host just connects a client.

Is MCP an orchestrator?

No. It is a connection protocol between a host and external tools. It does not plan or sequence agent behaviour.

How is MCP different from RAG?

They are unrelated ways to give a model context. RAG retrieves text and injects it into a prompt. MCP lets a model call tools and actions on external systems.

Can one server extend another, like inheritance?

Not in a code sense, but a server can contain an MCP client internally and forward requests to another server. Possible, not common.

How is a server deployed?

Like any other server: a plain process, a Docker container or a cloud service such as Cloud Run or AKS. MCP mandates no deployment method.

Can tool access be limited per user role?

In principle yes. The client requests the tool list, so the server can check the caller's auth token or scope before deciding which tools to return. MCP does not prescribe it; you build the check.

A company already has 25 to 30 working APIs. Why build an MCP server on top?

AI hosts speak MCP natively. Without a server, every team wanting AI to use those APIs writes and maintains its own wrapper, the duplication MCP exists to remove.

Do I need MCP for a small project?

Maybe not yet. One app and a handful of tools with nobody else reusing them is fine with plain function calling. MCP starts paying off once more than one app or team needs the same tool.

Is MCP an Anthropic product I pay for?

No. It is a free, open specification, now governed by a multi-company foundation. OpenAI and Google support it even though Anthropic built it first. "Agreed" is the key word: a protocol is a shared agreement, a library only works if everyone adopts one company's code.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Thinking MCP makes the model smarter Wrong expectations It widens what the model can see and do, not its reasoning
Believing one shared connection serves all servers Wrong architecture One client per server, 1:1
Calling MCP "just REST" Confusion about transports It is JSON-RPC 2.0 over STDIO or Streamable HTTP
Connecting many servers without limiting tools Huge token cost, confused agent Good descriptions and a filter
Treating a resource like a tool Wrong primitive Resources are read-only; tools have effects
Hard-coding shared reference data in each client Copies drift Expose it once as a resource
Using the old HTTP plus SSE transport Deprecated since the March 2025 spec Use Streamable HTTP
Skipping the docstring on a tool Poor description in the tool list Write one; FastMCP uses it

Hands-on lab

  1. Install uv, create mcp-warmup, add fastmcp and build the greet and add server.
  2. Run uv run fastmcp dev server.py and call both tools from Inspector.
  3. With Inspector connected, press Ctrl+C on the server and confirm only that connection closes.
  4. Register the same server in VS Code as STDIO and call a tool from chat.
  5. Optionally add it as a custom connector in Claude Desktop.
  6. Explain in your own words, to a friend, why a company with 500 teams benefits from one server.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

MCP is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools and data. Function calling worked for one app but meant every team rewrote and maintained the same integrations. With MCP, the provider runs one server and any host connects a client, so maintenance moves to the server owner. A host creates one client per server, they talk JSON-RPC 2.0 over STDIO locally or Streamable HTTP remotely, and a server offers three primitives: tools, resources and prompts.

Basics

What problem does MCP solve?

Function calling made every company wrap, authenticate and maintain the same tools on its own. At scale that is duplicated work that breaks when APIs change. MCP standardises the connection so the provider maintains one server and every host speaks to it the same way.

Define host, client and server.

The host is the AI application a person uses. The client is created inside the host and holds a dedicated 1:1 connection to one server. The server exposes tools, resources and prompts.

What are the three primitives?

Tools (actions that do something), resources (read-only data to read) and prompts (reusable templates that shape a request).

Which transports does MCP use?

STDIO for local servers and Streamable HTTP for remote ones. Streamable HTTP replaced HTTP plus SSE, deprecated in the March 2025 spec. The messages are JSON-RPC 2.0.

Intermediate

Why does each server get its own client?

Decoupling, safety (a crash stays contained), scalability (load is local to the pair) and parallelism (talk to several servers at once).

Why not just keep using function calling?

For one app and a few tools, you can. Beyond that the maintenance, auth and breakage burden repeats per team. MCP moves it to whoever owns the server.

Why is MCP not "USB-C for AI"?

The instructor felt it oversimplifies. An MCP server is a collection of tools (mostly) wrapped around existing APIs, plus resources and prompts, behind a shared protocol that decides who maintains what.

What is MCP Inspector?

A browser tool that connects to any MCP server (acting as host and client) so you can list and call its tools without a full AI app. Start it with uv run fastmcp dev server.py.

Resource vs tool?

A resource is read-only reference data with no side effects, like a thermostat display. A tool runs an action and has an effect. Use a resource when many clients need the same reference data, so there is one source of truth.

Tricky

MCP versus RAG?

Different mechanisms. RAG retrieves text and injects it into the prompt. MCP is a protocol for calling tools and actions on external systems. They are not usually compared directly.

What hidden cost comes with connecting many MCP servers?

The tool list from every server is sent on the first message, so tokens balloon (tens of thousands with two servers in the demo) and the agent can get confused. Reduce it with clear descriptions and by filtering tools with middleware.

How would you restrict a tool to some users?

Check the caller's auth token or scope in the server before returning the tool list or running the tool. MCP does not prescribe this; you build it.

Is MCP an orchestrator?

No. It is a communication protocol between host and external tools. It does not decide what happens next.

Why do OpenAI and Google support a protocol Anthropic created?

Because it is an open specification governed by a multi-company foundation. A protocol only works as an agreement everyone adopts, unlike a single company's library.

Part E MCP · Chapter 12

MCP primitives, lifecycle and JSON-RPC

The three primitives in working code, the three-phase MCP lifecycle, JSON-RPC 2.0 as the shared language, and the initialization handshake step by step.

Class 175 September45 min readCode: Weekend 10
Jump to a section

Why it matters

This is the chapter that separates someone who can use an MCP connector from someone who can explain how to build one that scales. Interview questions here are precise: "why JSON-RPC and not REST?", "what are the three handshake steps?", "what does the id field do?" The instructor's stated bar: be able to walk into a Google or Amazon interview and explain it.

Core ideas

1. Quick recap: why, and who talks to whom

People wanted ChatGPT-style AI connected to Google Drive, Slack, GitHub and Gmail. Defining custom tools for each did not scale, and MCP closed the gap. A host (Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, Codex) never talks to a server directly, because they do not share a language. It spins up a client per server, and the client and server communicate in JSON-RPC.

In the Inspector demo, Inspector is both host and client (the interface a person uses, and the thing opening the connection) while server.py is the server. The handshake the instant Inspector connects is a client doing its job.

Key ideaOne-to-one: which direction holds?

Each client connects to exactly one server. That always holds. The reverse depends on the transport. The official docs say: each MCP client maintains a dedicated, 1:1 connection with its server; local servers typically serve a single client, whereas remote servers typically serve many clients at once. A hosted Gmail or Slack MCP server is built for many clients.

Benefits of the 1:1 design (decoupling, safety, scalability, parallelism) were covered in Chapter 11. The safety proof: press Ctrl+C on the server while Inspector is connected and only that connection closes.

2. The three primitives

  • Tools are actions: the one primitive where the AI itself decides to act. Everything else is initiated by someone or something else first. Without a tool the AI can describe sending an email perfectly; with one it can send it.
  • Resources are read-only, near-static data: a repo's README, a database schema file, a team style guide in Google Drive, or (from MCP's own travel-planning example) a passport PDF or visa checklist. Typically the application, not the model, decides to read a resource and feed it in as context. A resource never changes anything.
  • Prompts are predefined templates that help the AI do a task well, not just do it. A bare create_issue call can produce a thin issue. A prompt guides the AI to gather a title, description and reproduction steps first, consistently. Only the form changed, not the model.
Common trapResources and prompts are optional

GitHub's official MCP server ships tools only, no resources or prompts, and that is a completely valid, common design. Tools are effectively the required primitive.

Primitive Functions What they do
Tools list, call list discovers tools and argument schemas; call invokes one
Resources list, read, subscribe list discovers; read retrieves one; subscribing tells a client when a resource changes
Prompts list, get list discovers templates; get retrieves one

The moment a client connects it calls the list functions (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list). That is how a host learns everything a server offers before using any of it.

3. All three in real code

Starting from the tools-only warm-up server, adding a resource and a prompt takes exactly two more decorators:

@mcp.resource("file://server-notes")
def server_notes() -> str:
    """Read-only notes about this server, straight from a local file."""
    with open("server-notes.txt") as f:
        return f.read()

@mcp.prompt
def structured_escalation(issue_summary: str, what_was_tried: str, customer_sentiment: str) -> str:
    """Guides the AI to log a customer escalation with every required field, in order."""
    return f"""Log this customer escalation with the following structure:
Issue Summary: {issue_summary}
What Was Already Tried: {what_was_tried}
Customer Sentiment: {customer_sentiment}
Recommended Next Action: [determine this from the details above]
"""

In Inspector: greet and add under Tools, file://server-notes under Resources (returning the file's real content), and structured_escalation under Prompts, asking for exactly the three fields. Filled in, it produces:

Issue Summary: Order #4521 arrived damaged
What Was Already Tried: Customer emailed support once, no reply in 3 days
Customer Sentiment: Frustrated, considering a refund request
Recommended Next Action: Escalate to logistics team, offer expedited replacement

Most tutorials stop at tools because tools are the easiest to demo. Resources and prompts are just as easy; they get skipped more often.

4. The lifecycle: three phases, always in this order

Initialization is the handshake and introduction, operation is the conversation, shutdown is saying goodbye. You cannot hold a conversation before anyone has been introduced.

To make it tangible, the instructor opened Claude Desktop's real MCP log (macOS: ~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp.log; Windows has an equivalent) showing actual JSON-RPC messages with a local Apple Notes server over STDIO. It also explains why a connector can show a warning icon before you use it: at startup Claude initialises every configured server, and if the handshake fails it already knows.

5. JSON-RPC 2.0: the shared language

Two systems need a common language, like two people. For client and server it is JSON-RPC 2.0. JSON is the familiar data format. RPC is Remote Procedure Call: run a function on another machine as if it were local, hiding the network details. Instead of specifying low-level query parameters, the client says "please query the DB with these arguments."

// Request (client to server)
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list", "params": {} }

// Response (server to client)
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": { "tools": [ ] } }
Field Meaning
jsonrpc Always "2.0": the format version both sides must agree on
id Matches a response to its request. Responses can arrive asynchronously and out of order, so without an id you could not tell which answers which
method, params What is being requested
result or error A response has one of these, never both

6. Why JSON-RPC and not plain REST?

An interview-level question, and the reasoning is deliberate.

Reason Meaning
Lightweight Plain, readable JSON without the headers and overhead of REST or XML
Transport-agnostic The same protocol works locally (STDIO) or remotely (HTTP)
Genuinely two-way The biggest departure. In HTTP, only the client initiates and the server replies. In JSON-RPC either side can initiate, so a server can proactively report progress on a long task instead of the client polling
Notifications built in A message with no id means "fire and expect nothing back", which strict request-response does not naturally support
Standard error codes Inherited wholesale, like HTTP's 404 and 500
Key ideaJSON-RPC is not an MCP invention

It is a pre-existing, general-purpose specification used elsewhere in networking. Anthropic adopted it because it already fit MCP's needs.

Common trapTwo-way is not the same as asynchronous, and not a WebSocket

Asynchronous means the client sends a request and carries on, expecting a reply later, but the server still never initiates. Two-way means either side can start a request. And it is not the same as a WebSocket: a WebSocket is a persistent always-open connection, heavier than most MCP interactions need. Two-way capability is a property of the JSON-RPC protocol, not of keeping a permanent socket.

7. The initialization handshake, step by step

  1. The client speaks first with its protocol version, capabilities and client info, tagged with an id (for example 1).
  2. The server responds, matching the id, with its protocol version, its capabilities (tools? resources? prompts?) and its server name.
  3. The client sends an initialized notification: no id, since no reply is expected. This is JSON-RPC notifications in action.

Two rules keep it orderly: the client should send nothing but a ping before the server responds to initialize, and the server should send nothing but a ping before it receives initialized.

8. Version and capability negotiation

The client always sends the latest version it supports, never a list of everything it has ever supported. If the server supports that exact version, it replies with the same one. If not, it replies with the latest it supports, and the client decides whether that is acceptable. With no overlap, they disconnect.

AnalogyWindows and a game negotiating DirectX

Windows supports DirectX 11. A game supports up to DirectX 8. They settle on the highest version both actually share, never a vague "I support all of them."

Real-world consequence, illustrated with WhatsApp: a message deleted in a newer version may not disappear correctly on an older one, because the versions disagree on behaviour. For a client built for a real company, it is not enough to connect to whatever URL is given. A serious implementation decides which historical protocol versions it supports and handles every behavioural difference. That depth is what a strong interview answer shows.

Key pointers to remember

  • MCP solves an integration problem, not an AI capability problem.
  • Host, client, server, always in that order.
  • Client to server is strictly one to one; server to client depends on transport.
  • Two decorators separate a tools-only server from one with all three primitives.
  • Service providers build servers; host developers build clients. Gmail's team builds the Gmail server; Anthropic builds the client in Claude.
  • Every primitive is discovered via its own list.
  • Lifecycle: initialization, operation, shutdown.
  • Handshake: initialize with id, response with the same id, initialized notification with no id.
  • The business case is N times M down to N plus M integrations: any compliant host talks to any compliant server without custom work.

Questions from class worth knowing

Can one MCP server call another?

Yes. A server can act as a client to another server internally, chaining them.

Is FastMCP the only way to build a server?

No. It is the most popular, alongside Anthropic's official MCP SDK. The relationship is like Keras on top of TensorFlow: the official SDK is the base and FastMCP makes building on it easier.

I already have REST APIs and a chatbot. Why build an MCP server?

The scalability maths. Connecting N applications to M tool sets means roughly N times M custom integrations. MCP standardises to about N plus M. It was candidly acknowledged that MCP can feel like needless abstraction over an API call; the value is making access usable by non-technical end users and cutting integration burden at scale.

How does a client know which server to connect to?

The address is given when the client is configured (like pasting a URL into "Add custom connector"). It is not discovered dynamically at connection time.

How does a server know which client a request came from?

That is resolved inside the transport layer: once connected, both sides keep session details internally, like any client-server connection, abstracted from the user.

How do I make my own email domain MCP compatible?

You cannot make an existing product inherently compatible. You build a normal MCP server for it exposing the tools, resources and prompts that make sense.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Assuming resources and prompts are required Over-building Tools are the essential primitive
Calling a resource a tool Wrong primitive Resources are read-only
Sending a list of supported versions Wrong negotiation Send only the latest
Forgetting id on a request Cannot match the response Always set it (notifications are the exception)
Replying to a notification Protocol error Notifications expect no reply
Treating two-way as a WebSocket Wrong design Two-way is a protocol property
Ignoring older protocol versions in a custom client Behaviour bugs across servers Decide and handle supported versions
Sending anything but pings before the handshake finishes Out-of-order protocol Wait for the handshake

Hands-on lab

  1. Redraw host, client and server from memory, marking where 1:1 applies.
  2. Add @mcp.resource and @mcp.prompt to the warm-up server and confirm all three in Inspector.
  3. Kill the server with Ctrl+C while Inspector is connected and watch it fail contained.
  4. Open your host's MCP log and find the three handshake messages.
  5. Write a JSON-RPC request and response pair by hand for a send_email call with a matching id.
  6. For a service you use daily, list what would be a tool, a resource and a prompt.
  7. Explain out loud why JSON-RPC was chosen over REST.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Client and server speak JSON-RPC 2.0, chosen over REST because it is lightweight, transport-agnostic, genuinely two-way and has notifications built in. A connection goes through initialization, operation and shutdown. Initialization is three steps: the client sends initialize with an id, the server responds with the same id and its capabilities, and the client sends an initialized notification with no id. A server offers tools, resources and prompts, each discovered with list.

Basics

What are the three MCP lifecycle phases?

Initialization (handshake and capability exchange), operation (the real work) and shutdown (closing the connection, usually initiated by the client).

What are the three handshake steps?

The client sends initialize with an id, protocol version and capabilities. The server responds with the same id, its version, capabilities and name. The client sends an initialized notification with no id, which expects no reply.

What is the id field for?

It matches a response to its request. Responses can arrive asynchronously and out of order, so without an id you cannot tell which answers which.

Which primitive lets the AI act?

Tools. Resources are read by the application and prompts are chosen by the user or app, so the tool is the one the model decides to use.

Intermediate

Why JSON-RPC instead of REST?

Lightweight JSON, transport-agnostic (STDIO or HTTP), two-way so a server can initiate (for example progress on long tasks), notifications with no id, and standard error codes.

JSON-RPC two-way vs asynchronous vs WebSocket?

Async means the client fires and continues but the server never initiates. Two-way means either side can initiate. A WebSocket is a persistent open connection, which is heavier; two-way is a protocol property and does not require it.

How does version negotiation work?

The client sends the latest version it supports. If the server supports it, it echoes it. Otherwise it replies with its latest and the client decides if that is acceptable. With no overlap, they disconnect. Never send a list.

Is JSON-RPC an MCP invention?

No. It is an existing general-purpose spec that Anthropic adopted because it fit.

What does a client do first after connecting?

Calls the list functions (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list) to learn what the server offers before using any of it.

Tricky

Can a server serve more than one client?

Yes. A client has exactly one server, but a remote server typically serves many clients. Local STDIO servers typically serve one.

Why might a connector show a warning icon before you use it?

At startup the host initialises every configured server. If the handshake fails, it already knows and flags it.

Why must a serious custom client think about older protocol versions?

Versions can behave differently, like WhatsApp message deletion across versions. A production client must decide which versions it supports and handle each behavioural difference, not just connect to any URL.

What can be sent before the handshake completes?

Only pings: the client before the server responds to initialize, and the server before it receives initialized.

What is the business case for MCP in numbers?

N applications by M tool sets means about N times M custom integrations. A standard protocol reduces that to about N plus M, because any compliant host talks to any compliant server.

Part E MCP · Chapter 13

Capability negotiation and the operation phase

Both sides hand over an honest menu, the client discovers and calls tools, the server can ask the user for missing information (elicitation), and a wiretap script lets you watch the real JSON-RPC conversation.

Class 18 (transcript)6 September45 min readCode: Weekend 10
Jump to a section
Repo noteClass numbers differ between the two summary sets

The transcript summaries number this session Class 18 and the short summaries call it Class 17. They are the same 6 September class. The code folder is Weekend 10.

Why it matters

"It just works" is a bad answer in an interview. Things fail at exactly these points in production: capability negotiation, discovery and calls. This chapter shows each step on real systems, plus a tool that makes the hidden JSON-RPC visible. It also covers the question every MCP user eventually asks: are we exposing our data to the LLM?

Core ideas

1. Capability negotiation: an honest menu

Key ideaBoth sides hand over a menu before anyone orders

Client and server each declare what they are capable of, not what they are about to do. That way each side knows what it can ask for later. It is not a commitment; nothing is used until needed.

Side Capability Meaning
Client roots Ability to expose file-system access
Client sampling Supports an LLM sampling request
Client elicitation Can ask the user on the server's behalf
Client tasks, experimental Task support; non-standard features
Server tools, resources, prompts The three primitives
Server logging Can send log messages
Server completions Argument auto-completion
Server experimental Non-standard features

2. Elicitation: the server asks the client

Here the two-way nature of JSON-RPC becomes concrete. Elicitation is how a server requests additional information from the user, through the client, mid-interaction. It does not only reply; it reaches out for something it needs. In LangChain's docs, elicitation surfaces as a LangGraph interrupt: a human answers it and the run resumes.

Common trapElicitation is not Human-in-the-Loop

HITL is an AI-lifecycle safety mechanism layered on tool calls (approve, edit, reject). Elicitation is a native MCP mechanism for a server to ask for information it is missing. Different concept, easy to confuse.

On "deprecated". An older communication pattern is marked deprecated in the newest spec. Deprecated does not mean unused: most servers in the wild still run the older pattern, and migrating an ecosystem takes close to a year.

3. Watching it happen for real

  • VS Code with Context7. Adding the server showed connect then discover tools, automatically, before any request. Context7 is a useful, authentication-free server that returns the latest documentation for a library, solving the problem of a model's training data lagging a fast-moving API. It was named one of the top five most-used MCP servers.
  • Claude Desktop with Apple Notes. The real tool list appeared: list_notes, get_note_content, add_note, update_note_content, with Claude aware of each before any note question.

None of this discovery is written by hand; it is baked into the architecture. You still need to understand every step because production fails at these exact points, and someone who only knows "it just works" cannot diagnose why it stopped.

4. The operation phase: discovery and calling

Operation is exactly two steps.

Step Method When Cost
Discovery tools/list Automatically the instant the handshake completes, before any user question Free: no LLM involved, just the client asking the server what it offers
Calling tools/call Only when a request needs a specific tool Needs a tool name and arguments

A real example. Asked to "list my Apple Notes", the logs showed the real list_notes schema: a folder argument (string, optional, "filter notes by folder") and a limit (number, default 20). Requesting the "Personal" folder sent folder: "Personal" and no limit, so the server's default of 20 applied. Every tool on every server (Gmail, Calendar, Notes) has this same shape: a name, a description and an input schema. The quality of the description decides whether the AI picks the right tool at all.

Key ideaNegotiation says a category exists. Discovery says what is in it.

A student asked why the client calls tools/list if negotiation already said the server "has tools". Negotiation only confirms tools exist as a category. It says nothing about which tools, their names or their arguments. Discovery retrieves that detail.

Errors. Malformed requests fail loudly as a proper JSON-RPC error object using standard codes (a wrong tool name gives a "method not found" style error). This is the same point where the tool-error and retry middleware from Chapter 8 apply.

5. The privacy trade-off, head on

"So with MCP, we are exposing our data to the LLM?" Yes. Whatever a tool returns, the client hands to the host, which sends it to the model provider to generate a response. This is real information flow.

  • It is a legitimate reason to lock down which notes, files or folders a connection can see. Apple Notes' lock feature was demoed: a locked note becomes invisible to any MCP call.
  • On the developer's side, middleware (PII detection, guardrails before a model call) controls what the model sees in a custom client or server. See Chapters 7 and 8.

6. Debugging: seeing real JSON-RPC

A third-party "playground" inspector made the lifecycle visible on a two-tool server (getCurrentTime, convertTime). "Convert the current Indian time to Chicago time" produced: an LLM call to understand, tools/call to getCurrentTime, a second LLM call to interpret, tools/call to convertTime, and a final LLM call to answer. The exact request and response bodies were visible, with ids incrementing on every call regardless of primitive.

Common trapClaude Desktop stopped logging full JSON bodies

The repo's wiretap script documents the change. As of 26 June 2026, Claude Desktop's mcp.log and mcp-server-*.log stopped writing the full JSON of each message and now log only a terse one-line summary (method, id, whether params or a result are present). Entries before that date have full JSON; entries after do not. This is the client changing how much it writes to disk, not an MCP protocol version change. Two separate things.

7. The wiretap: sit in the middle of the conversation

Instead of reading logs afterwards, mcp_wiretap.py sits in the conversation. Claude Desktop launches the wiretap instead of the real server, the wiretap launches the real server, and it relays every byte unchanged while printing a pretty copy of each message. Claude Desktop never knows.

In claude_desktop_config.json, change the server entry. Everything after -- is the real command that used to be there:

"filesystem": {
  "command": "python3",
  "args": [
    "/absolute/path/to/mcp_wiretap.py",
    "--log", "/path/to/wiretap-live.log",
    "--", "npx", "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/you/Desktop"
  ]
}

Fully quit Claude Desktop (Cmd+Q), reopen, and use it normally. The terminal (or log file) shows the handshake, capability discovery, every tool call and shutdown. A --no-color variant exists for piping to a file.

Pro tipGenericise paths before copying

The repo ships claude_desktop_config.example.json with generic paths. Do not copy a real machine's paths into a shared config.

8. Legacy vs modern in the real world

In the debugging tool's connection log, connecting to an older unmigrated server first tried a newer discovery call, got an error because the server did not recognise it, then fell back to the older initialize-first handshake and succeeded. That is version negotiation working in real time.

Realistic migration to a newer MCP version takes 8 months to a year for most servers, with only actively maintained ones (LangChain's, for instance) moving in the first couple of months. A client must support both the modern and legacy handshakes, not only the newest. That separates a demo from something built for a company. Chapter 17 compares them in full.

9. Why MCP and not just function calling (again)

Function calling is fine for a small single-app project. MCP earns its keep once more than one application or team reuses the same tool: a service builds its connector once and every compliant app uses it. It is a free, open, multi-company-governed specification, not a paid Anthropic product, which is why OpenAI and Google support it. Only a shared agreement gets adopted broadly enough to matter.

10. Live project: a no-code AI news updater

Gmail, Google Calendar, Tavily and Apple Notes were connected as live MCP servers through Claude's connector settings. Claude turned a rough flow diagram into a system prompt that researches AI news via Tavily, categorises it, drafts an HTML email, creates a recurring calendar reminder and produces a LinkedIn post and a Substack article.

Key ideaThe brain decides. Tools act.

The model is used every time a decision is needed: which tool, which arguments, how to interpret a result. Data movement happens only through tool calls. A calendar event is created by a tool call once the model picks a time. Search results are woven into a narrative by the model, never by the search tool. Same agentic loop as the start of the course, now across four independent services.

Pro tipA prompt-writing lesson from the same demo

Without telling the model how many headlines to include per category, it made its own undocumented assumption and quietly dropped real stories. The fix is not a framework feature. Be explicit about how much detail you want and test until it holds.

11. An enterprise scenario, worked through

A DevOps architect managing 150+ microservices across AWS, Azure and GCP wanted a vulnerability-remediation agent, but their enterprise Claude account had connector installation locked down to stop data leaving the organisation. The guidance: this is exactly the case for a custom MCP server. A self-hosted server (possibly its own Docker container, fitting the multi-cloud container pipeline) keeps sensitive data inside the organisation, since nothing passes through a third-party connector.

Key pointers to remember

  • Negotiation is an honest menu, not a commitment.
  • Elicitation is a server asking for missing information, native to MCP and different from HITL.
  • Discovery is automatic and free; calling needs a name and arguments.
  • Data returned by a tool really goes to the model provider.
  • A deprecated version still runs most servers; support both handshakes.
  • MCP is a free multi-company specification.
  • The brain decides; tools act.

Questions from class worth knowing

How do we restrict specific tools for specific users in an MCP setup?

That is not an MCP-architecture concern. It is ordinary software engineering, solved with middleware (the guardrail and dynamic tool loading patterns from earlier chapters), not a built-in MCP feature.

Can I create my own MCP server inside Claude?

No. You can connect your own server to Claude, but Claude is not where you build and host one.

Does calling an MCP tool cost LLM tokens?

No. A tool call is a plain client-server transaction. Tokens are spent only when the model is invoked to reason or generate.

Does MCP have built-in caching?

Not by default as far as could be confirmed live. If you want caching, build it separately.

Are Claude's "connectors" the same as MCP servers?

Yes. Claude uses friendlier words ("connectors", "tools") for a general audience to avoid confusing non-technical users.

Should I claim a "production-grade" AI project on my resume if it was not deployed at scale?

Describe it honestly and frame it around the real problem it solved, not the technology. Interviewers care about problem-solving depth, and shallow claims are exposed quickly under questioning.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Skipping tools/list because negotiation said "tools" Not knowing the tool names or arguments Always run discovery
Thinking discovery uses the LLM Wrong cost estimates It is free; no model involved
Confusing elicitation with HITL Wrong mechanism chosen Elicitation is a server asking for info; HITL approves tool calls
Assuming returned data stays local Privacy surprise It goes to the model provider; restrict and filter
Reading Claude Desktop logs for message bodies Only one-line summaries Use the wiretap
Supporting only the newest handshake Fails against most servers Support legacy and modern
Vague tool description Wrong tool chosen Write a precise description
Not specifying detail level in prompts Silently dropped content State exactly what you want

Hands-on lab

  1. Add Context7 to VS Code and watch discovery happen on connect.
  2. Trigger a tools/list and a tools/call yourself and read both bodies.
  3. Compare an older and a newer entry in your own mcp.log.
  4. Run mcp_wiretap.py in front of a server you already use and read the traffic.
  5. Try the playground inspector on a two-tool server and trace one multi-step request.
  6. Build a no-code mini-project with at least three real connectors and note where the model's own assumptions shape the output.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Capability negotiation is each side declaring what it can do, an honest menu, not a commitment. Then the operation phase has two steps: discovery with tools/list, which is automatic and costs no tokens, and calling with tools/call, which needs a name and arguments. Servers can also elicit information from the user through the client. Everything a tool returns is shared with the model provider, so I restrict and filter data deliberately.

Basics

What is capability negotiation?

Both sides declare what they are capable of so each knows what it may ask for later. Client capabilities include roots, sampling, elicitation, tasks and experimental. Server capabilities include tools, resources, prompts, logging, completions and experimental.

What is elicitation?

A server requesting additional information from the user, through the client, mid-interaction. In LangChain it appears as a LangGraph interrupt that a human answers before the run resumes.

What are the two steps of the operation phase?

Discovery (tools/list, automatic and free) and calling (tools/call, needing a tool name and arguments).

Does discovery cost tokens?

No. No LLM is involved. It is just the client asking the server what it offers.

Intermediate

Why call tools/list if negotiation already says there are tools?

Negotiation confirms tools exist as a category. Discovery retrieves which tools, their descriptions and argument schemas.

Elicitation vs HITL?

HITL is an approval layer over tool calls (approve, edit, reject, respond). Elicitation is a native MCP mechanism for the server to request missing information from the client and user.

Are we exposing data to the LLM with MCP?

Yes. Tool results flow client to host to model provider. That is why you restrict what a connection can see (for example locked notes), and use PII middleware and guardrails on custom clients.

What does a good tool definition contain?

A name, a description and an input schema. The description quality decides whether the model picks the right tool.

How should a client handle old and new servers?

Try the newer handshake, fall back to the older one on an error, and explicitly support both. Most servers take 8 months to a year to migrate.

Tricky

Claude Desktop's logs used to show full JSON and now do not. Did the protocol change?

No. The client changed how much it writes to disk (from 26 June 2026 it logs only a terse summary). It is unrelated to the MCP version. The wiretap script recovers the full conversation.

How does the wiretap work?

It sits between Claude Desktop and the real server. Claude Desktop launches the wiretap, which launches the real server and relays every byte unchanged while printing each message. You put the real command after -- in the config.

How would you build a vulnerability agent when connectors are locked down?

A custom self-hosted MCP server, possibly containerised, so sensitive data never leaves the organisation through a third-party connector.

A multi-service no-code workflow dropped some stories. Why?

The model made its own undocumented assumption about how many items to include. Be explicit about the detail wanted in the prompt, and test.

Is "brain decides, tools act" still true across many services?

Yes. The model decides which tool, arguments and how to interpret results. Data movement only happens through tool calls.
